findings.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The recovery-authn-codes credential provider is looked up by a hardcoded string "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" instead of RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID. If the provider id constant is ever renamed in services (where RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory lives), session.getProvider silently returns null here and every non-userStorage recovery-code creation throws an NPE at required-action time; a maintainer grepping for usages of PROVIDER_ID will miss this call site entirely.

[ADVISORY] The fallback calls recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential without a null check on the provider obtained from a string-id lookup that can return null (e.g. if the RECOVERY_CODES feature/provider is disabled in the deployment). When the recovery-codes feature is disabled but a custom userStorage returns false from updateCredential, users hit a NullPointerException (500) instead of a clean error; the provider was previously fetched via the typed factory constant in RecoveryAuthnCodesAction, where a missing provider was at least surfaced consistently.

[BUG] getCredential returns only the single first matching credential, and prefers federated credentials unconditionally over local ones even when both exist. For a user who has recovery codes in BOTH userStorage and local DB (the exact mixed state this feature makes reachable: local codes created before the userStorage started supporting the type), getCredential returns the federated credential while the login form's code numbering and the authenticator's validation use only that credential — a locally-generated valid code is rejected with INVALID_CREDENTIALS, locking the user out of half their issued codes with no error indicating the split state.

[ADVISORY] The refactor preserves the pre-existing Optional.get() on the result of RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential, which returns Optional.empty() when neither federated nor local recovery codes exist. A user whose userStorage supports the type but has no recovery codes stored (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isConfiguredFor returns false, yet the authenticator is REQUIRED in the new flow) reaches this bean and gets a NoSuchElementException instead of a challenge page — the failure now also covers the federated-miss path the old code could not hit, so the unreachable-.get() assumption no longer holds.

[ADVISORY] getCredentials stores the locally-reconstructed RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel (built via createFromValues, which hashes the codes into secretData) into the returned stream, but the same method's deserialization failure branch silently omits the credential from the stream instead of surfacing the error. If the userStorage's stored JSON is ever corrupted (or a code list element deserializes as non-String), the user's recovery codes silently vanish from the credential manager's view: getCredential returns empty, the required-action re-triggers, and the user is asked to regenerate codes while isValid in the same provider still validates against the corrupted store — a debugging dead end with only a log.error and no failure to the caller.

[ADVISORY] JsonSerialization failure is wrapped in a bare RuntimeException with no message, discarding the operation context. Serializing a List<String> practically cannot fail, but if it ever does (custom module swapping the Jackson mapper), the operator gets an unattributed RuntimeException on the required-action path with no username or realm to correlate, unlike the logged context on the success paths.

[BUG] The userStorage recovery-code validation never consumes or marks a code as used, so every generated code can be replayed indefinitely. A user (or an attacker who has captured one code) can authenticate with the same recovery code forever; the core acceptance criterion of recovery authn codes — single-use, one of N consumptions — is silently dropped for all user-storage users, and neither the diff's helper nor the new test verifies code non-reuse (the test logs in once and never attempts a second login with the same code).

[BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential stores the raw generated codes as plaintext JSON in the user storage with no hashing, unlike the local-storage path which persists a hashed RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel. Every user-storage provider adopting this path receives and must persist the cleartext recovery codes; a storage compromise exposes all codes directly, and the two sibling paths in the same method apply different security semantics for the same credential type with no documented requirement stating the plaintext handoff is intentional.

[BUG] credentialModelOpt.get() is called without isPresent() handling, throwing NoSuchElementException when a user has no recovery-code credential in either federated or local storage. Rendering the recovery-code login page for a user whose storage provider returns an empty credential stream (e.g. storage backed by an older provider that does not implement getCredentials, or a user who never set codes up but the authenticator is still triggered) crashes with a 500 instead of failing the flow gracefully; the diff restructured this line to Optional but retained the unguarded get().

[ADVISORY] The local-storage fallback branch of createRecoveryCodesCredential (userStorageCreated == false) has no test coverage anywhere in the diff. testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only exercises the userStorage-created path (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage returns true); a regression in the else-branch — e.g. provider lookup by the string literal "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" drifting from RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID — would break recovery-code setup for all users on storages that don't support the type, with no failing test to catch it; the string literal also bypasses the constant the same diff removed from RecoveryAuthnCodesAction.

[ADVISORY] getCredentials silently swallows the IOException from deserializing the stored recovery-code credential and returns a stream omitting it, with only a log.error. A user whose stored credential JSON is corrupted becomes unable to log in with recovery codes with no surfaced error beyond a server log line; the login flow then treats the credential as absent and the user gets INVALID_CREDENTIALS with no diagnostic — an operator debugging a broken storage sees user-visible auth failure uncorrelated with the root cause.

[ADVISORY] assertUserHasRecoveryKeysCredentialInUserStorage ignores its userId parameter and hardcodes the username "otp1" when querying the storage factory. Any future caller passing a different user (or a reused test with another username, as addUserAndResetPassword already takes an arbitrary username) gets a false pass/fail against the wrong user's state; the next test author extending this helper is bitten by an assertion that checks a different user than the one under test.

[ADVISORY] The new test never verifies the logoutOtherSessions=false variant of setupRecoveryKeysForUserWithRequiredAction nor the delayed-authenticator branch configured in configureBrowserFlowWithRecoveryAuthnCodes (the delay parameter is always passed as 0). The helper accepts and the flow builder configures behavior (session-revocation skipping, delayed-brute-force-count code path) that no assertion in this diff exercises, so regressions there ship silently while the plumbing suggests coverage; a future change breaking the non-logout variant of recovery-code setup would pass this suite.

[ADVISORY] The diff modifies BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage, violating the provider's own documented invariant that it represents an unmodified Keycloak 4.8.3-era user storage implementation. The whole point of this provider (per its class javadoc: 'Future Keycloak versions should work fine without a need to change the code of this provider') is to prove old third-party user storages keep working against new Keycloak versions; by adding recovery-codes support directly to it, the test suite no longer exercises the actual contract this PR claims to support — an old provider without recovery-codes support, where updateCredential returns false and the code should silently fall back to local Keycloak storage. Anyone relying on this test as evidence that recovery codes work with legacy user storages gets a false signal; the new-method fallback path (updateCredential returning false) is never tested with a legacy-style provider.

[ADVISORY] The diff adds `newOTP.setId(KeycloakModelUtils.generateId())` to the OTP updateCredential path, an unrelated behavior change not traceable to the recovery-key requirement. This is a silent fix/behavior change in the OTP credential-update path smuggled into a recovery-keys PR; it changes the ID assignment behavior of OTP credentials created through this provider and is undocumented in the PR intent, so a future maintainer bisecting an OTP ID regression lands on a PR titled 'recovery key support' and cannot connect it to any requirement.

[ADVISORY] configureBrowserFlowWithRecoveryAuthnCodes takes a `delay` parameter and installs a 'delayed-authenticator' execution, but the only caller passes 0, so the delay machinery is dead code copied from another test. The next maintainer of this test copies the pattern believing the delay is load-bearing; the parameter and the delayed-authenticator execution can be deleted outright (the flow works identically with delay=0), making this speculative generality in a test that should mirror the real login flow.

[ADVISORY] createRecoveryCodesCredential does not pass generatedCodes to the local-storage fallback path, so codes stored locally and codes stored in user storage are represented by two different mechanisms (credentialModel vs. raw JSON in challengeResponse) with no shared source of truth. A user-storage implementation receiving the UserCredentialModel gets the raw codes JSON in challengeResponse while the local path stores the hashed RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel; any code that later reads the credential must know which representation it holds, and the BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid comparison (`key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())`) only works because the same raw-codes representation is round-tripped — a second storage provider that hashes or transforms the challengeResponse breaks login validation invisibly.

[BUG] The userStorage fallback writes the raw generated codes as a plain JSON list into the credential's data, but every consumer of the federated credential (RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean, RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator, account REST) parses that data with RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel, which expects the model's own schema (hashed codes, remaining count, next-code numbering) — the two paths disagree on the wire format of the same credential type. A user whose recovery codes live in userStorage hits the login page: RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean.createFromCredentialModel(credentialModelOpt.get()) deserializes a bare JSON array as the model's credential-data object, so getNextRecoveryAuthnCode() returns empty/throws (NoSuchElementException on .get()) and the recovery-code login page 500s instead of rendering; the form authenticator's createFromCredentialModel on the same raw credential produces a model with no hashed codes so verification against it cannot succeed.

[BUG] The userStorage validation path never consumes or invalidates a used recovery code — isValid() checks the entered code against the full stored list and no code in this diff marks a code as used on the federated path, while the local-storage path decrements remaining codes through RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider. A recovery code captured by an attacker (or shoulder-surfed) grants unlimited logins for a userStorage-backed user, because the same code matches forever; the one-time-use invariant that the local credential model enforces is unrepresentable in the shape CredentialHelper.writeCredential chose (a flat list with no used/remaining state).

[ADVISORY] Recovery codes are stored hashed (in the model's secretData) when they land in local storage but as a plaintext JSON list in the userStorage path, so the same logical credential has two divergent representations depending on where it lands. Any userStorage provider adopting this contract inherits a plaintext-copy-of-all-recovery-codes obligation, and code that later migrates, rotates, or audits credentials must handle two formats for one type; the provider author writing updateCredential has no typed contract telling them which shape Keycloak will send.

[ADVISORY] getCredential() silently prefers a federated credential over a local one with no detection of, or handling for, both existing, and callers like RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean still call Optional.get() on its result. If a user ever has recovery codes in both stores (e.g. set locally before being linked to userStorage, or a provider that half-handles updateCredential returns false on a later rotation), the stale local copy is silently ignored, and if neither store has the credential the Optional machinery gained in this refactor still ends in an unconditional .get() that throws NoSuchElementException — the Optional adds no safety over the code it replaced.

[ADVISORY] updateCredential() is a generic 'update any credential' SPI method being used as a 'create recovery codes' probe — its boolean return means 'the provider handled this credential input', and any userStorage provider that accepts the type but fails internally still returns true, so the local-storage fallback is skipped with no error surfaced. A provider that accepts the recovery-codes type but stores nothing (a stub or partial implementation) causes the required action to report success while the user has no usable credential anywhere — the user is locked out at next login with no error at creation time; there is no verification that what the provider stored is retrievable.

[BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential silently discards the hashed RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel when the user storage accepts the credential, persisting the raw generated codes as plaintext JSON instead. For users in a user storage that accepts updateCredential, recovery codes are stored in cleartext (the credentialData field of the UserCredentialModel carries JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)) rather than the hashed representation the required action previously produced, while local-storage users still get hashed credentials — the recovery-codes hashing guarantee established by the existing intent is dropped for the federated path without any explicit acceptance of that downgrade; anyone with read access to the federated store reads usable recovery codes directly.

[BUG] The branch for user-storage users writes raw JSON via a bare UserCredentialModel while the fallback branch writes the full hashed credentialModel, producing two incompatible credential shapes for the same credential type with no migration or documented acceptance of the divergence. RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator's getCredential → RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel path now receives, for federated users, a CredentialModel whose credentialData is a raw list of codes rather than the hashed model structure (hashedCodes, remainingCodes, etc.), so the form authenticator's parsing/consumption logic built for the hashed shape operates on a payload it was never designed for — the single-credential-type contract that all consumers assumed is silently forked by this diff.

[ADVISORY] The required action's one-time-use semantics for recovery codes are silently dropped for user-storage users: processAction now delegates to createRecoveryCodesCredential, which on the federated path stores the raw code list and never applies the used-code consumption tracking that the local CredentialProvider path applies. A user whose storage provider handles the update (as the modified BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage does) gets recovery codes that pass isValid on every use since the federated isValid compares against the full raw list and nothing decrements/marks codes used — the product-level intent that recovery codes are single-use is not preserved on this path, and an attacker who observes one code can reuse it indefinitely.

[ADVISORY] This diff repurposes BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage — whose documented intent (class javadoc, unchanged in this diff) is to be an unmodified Keycloak-4.8.3-era provider verifying old providers keep working — into an actively extended provider with new recovery-codes support. The class's entire reason to exist (backwards-compatibility canary for untouched legacy provider code) is contradicted by adding supportsCredentialType/updateCredential/getCredentials branches for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE; the next developer reading the javadoc trusts this file is frozen 4.8.3 code, and the compatibility guarantee it was meant to prove is no longer being tested.

[BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw, un-hashed recovery codes (generatedCodes) into the credential's challengeResponse and hands them to the user-storage provider, so recovery codes are persisted in cleartext in federated storage. The local Keycloak provider stores recovery codes hashed (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues), but this new user-storage path bypasses that: the raw code list is sent verbatim via updateCredential, and any storage provider that stores it (as the shipped BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage does at BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java line ~192, setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse())) writes usable, plaintext recovery codes to the external store — a database read or backup leak of the federation store yields working single-factor login credentials for every federated user.

[BUG] isValid() for recovery codes performs a plain equality match against the stored list but never removes or marks the consumed code as used, making recovery codes infinitely replayable in the federated path. In the local-storage path, Keycloak's RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider invalidates a used code (the credential model's remaining-codes list is decremented on successful auth). The user-storage path added by this diff has no equivalent: the test demonstrates that a federated user can submit the same recovery code on every subsequent login forever, defeating the single-use guarantee that recovery codes exist to provide — an attacker who observes one code (e.g. shoulder-surf or a leaked page) gets permanent second-factor access. The product-side helper (CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential) provides no consumed-code update mechanism for user storage, so this gap is structural, not test-only.

[ADVISORY] The recovery-code comparison generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())) uses a non-constant-time String.equals, and the federated-codes contract it demonstrates exposes raw codes to the provider at all. Whoever copies this pattern as a reference implementation for custom user-storage recovery-code validation inherits both a timing side-channel and plaintext handling of the secret; since Keycloak's local provider compares hashed values with constant-time MessageDigest.isEqual, the federated example silently downgrades the security posture for implementers who mirror it.

[ADVISORY] testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin exercises only the happy path of the new federated recovery-code flow and never asserts single-use/invalidation semantics or rejection of a wrong code, so the new isValid/never-consumes behavior in BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java:326-345) is verified only for the success branch. The BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid implementation compares the submitted code against the raw stored list with anyMatch and never removes the used code, while the local-storage provider (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider) invalidates each used code; the test logs in with code index 0 exactly once and asserts only appPage.assertCurrent(), so a regression where federated recovery codes are reusable indefinitely (or where a wrong code is accepted) passes this suite — users of user-storage providers get recovery codes that never burn, an attacker-class weakness in the credential this test claims to certify.

[ADVISORY] The new fallback branch in CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential (server-spi-private/.../CredentialHelper.java:112-130, the `userStorageCreated == false` path calling recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential) has no test in this diff. Checked BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.java (the only test file changed): all added assertions target a user whose updateCredential returns true, so assertUserDontHaveDBCredentials always runs against the userStorage path; if the fallback-to-local-DB branch regresses (e.g., wrong provider id or dropped credentialModel), the diff's test still passes and a user whose storage declines the credential silently gets no recovery codes at all.

[ADVISORY] The IOException catch in BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials swallows the error and silently returns a stream omitting the recovery credential, and no test in the diff triggers a malformed credentialData to verify downstream behavior. If the stored JSON is ever corrupt (e.g., a version skew or the empty-id UserCredentialModel path in CredentialHelper.writeValueAsString changing shape), getCredential in RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils returns Optional.empty and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean throws NoSuchElementException at credentialModelOpt.get() (RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean.java:22) — a 500 on the login page; the swallowing log-only branch means this failure mode is invisible to the diff's green test.

[BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential passes the plaintext JSON list of raw codes to user storage via UserCredentialModel.getChallengeResponse(), while the local-DB path persists the hashed RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel — the same credential type carries two incompatible payloads depending on which storage handled the write. Any user storage that generically persists the challengeResponse (the documented contract for updateCredential inputs) stores un-hashed codes, and consumers reading via getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream/createFromCredentialModel on such a stored model fail to parse hashed-format credentialData — recovery code validation and display break for those users with no migration path to repair the mixed representations already written.

[ADVISORY] The credential is written to exactly one side: when the user storage accepts updateCredential, no local-DB copy of the hashed credential is created, so there is no dual-write during the cutover to federated recovery codes. An operator who later un-links or removes the user storage provider (a standard migration) silently loses every federated user's recovery codes — users fall back to no second factor with no error, a data-loss-on-migration scenario the diff neither backs up nor detects.

[BUG] RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean calls credentialModelOpt.get() on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential, which is empty when a user has no recovery-codes credential in either federated or local storage. A user whose required recovery-codes flow reaches this bean without a credential (e.g., the credential was deleted between the required action and the login, or a storage returns an empty getCredentials stream) gets an unhandled NoSuchElementException and a 500 login page instead of a fallback to another authenticator in the alternative subflow.

[ADVISORY] isValid for the recovery-codes type compares the entered code against the stored plain list and never consumes or updates the stored credential, so recovery codes validated through the user storage remain valid forever. The test asserts the happy-path login works, but the single-use semantics that the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider enforces (used-code counters in the credential data) are silently lost for federated users — anyone replaying a captured recovery code on the federated path is accepted, and tests built on this provider will pass while production semantics diverge.

[BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential wraps the IOException from JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString in a bare RuntimeException, aborting the required-action with an unhandled 500 after the user has already been shown the one-time recovery codes. If JSON serialization of the generated codes list fails, the user's browser shows the recovery codes page, clicks save, and gets a raw 500 (no INVALID_CREDENTIALS/controlled challenge, no error page per the required-action contract); the codes were displayed but never persisted, and the required action is silently left pending, so the user is stuck in a loop of generating codes that are never stored.

[BUG] When the user storage accepts the credential (userStorageCreated == true), the hashed RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel is discarded and the plaintext generated codes are delivered via challengeResponse, so any user storage implementing updateCredential persists the raw codes with no hashed form anywhere. For user-storage users, the only persisted copy of recovery codes is the plaintext JSON in challengeResponse. When the credential is later consumed (a code used at login), Keycloak's consumption path updates via a RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel whose serialized credentialData is the hashed format, and the storage's later getCredentials/isValid deserializes it as List.class — readValue(List.class) on the hashed JSON object structure fails (IOException path) or the codes never match, so single-use consumption silently breaks for federated users after the first code use.

[ADVISORY] getCredential prefers the federated credential unconditionally and only falls back to local storage when no federated credential exists, so a user with both a stale local recovery-codes credential and a fresh federated one authenticates against whichever the federated lookup returns first with no staleness check. Operators migrating a user from user storage to local storage (or vice versa) end up with two live recovery-code sets; the hidden one remains valid for the form authenticator's updateCredential-driven consumption path and for account-REST delete operations targeting the local credential, leaving an orphaned still-usable credential that no one can enumerate.

[BUG] The rewritten constructor still calls credentialModelOpt.get() on an Optional that getCredential can return empty, throwing NoSuchElementException instead of a controlled failure. A user whose recovery-codes credential is deleted (or whose user storage returns it via a path that isConfiguredFor accepts but getCredential filters out, e.g. a type-mismatched federated record) reaches the login form renderer and gets a raw 500 from template rendering rather than the configured invalid-credentials challenge.

[ADVISORY] getCredentials silently drops the recovery-codes credential on deserialization failure, logging a message without the exception or username and still returning the OTP-only stream. If myUser.recoveryCodes.getCredentialData() is corrupt (e.g. after a consumption update stores the hashed JSON format that readValue(List.class) cannot parse), the user appears to have no recovery codes at all: isConfiguredFor still returns true (it checks the raw field) but the credential stream is empty, so getCredential() returns empty and the login bean throws NoSuchElementException — a silent partial-success state that the error log alone makes undiagnosable.

[ADVISORY] isValid for recovery codes matches the submitted code against the full stored list without ever removing or marking the used code, so recovery codes are infinitely reusable. Any generated code authenticates the federated user an unlimited number of times, defeating the single-use guarantee the recovery-codes feature promises; the new test logs in once and never asserts a second use of the same code fails, so this regression is invisible to the suite.

[ADVISORY] hasRecoveryCodes looks up userPasswords.get(username) directly, bypassing the translateUserName normalization every other access path in the storage applies. If the user is created or stored under a differently-cased name than the assertion helper passes, the factory returns false for a user who does have recovery codes, making assertUserHasRecoveryKeysCredentialInUserStorage fail (or pass vacuously) with no signal that the lookup itself was wrong.

goldens.comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

If `getProvider(...)` returns null (e.g., provider not registered/feature disabled or ID mismatch), and `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` returns false, this will throw a NullPointerException. The diff clearly introduces this new null-dereference risk in the fallback branch.

adjudication.rationale: In `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential`, the code explicitly searches federated credentials first and returns only the first match, falling back to local stored credentials only if no federated credential exists: `.getFederatedCredentialsStream()...findFirst().or(() -> ...getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...).findFirst())`. This preference is then used by both the authenticator (`RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator`) and the login bean (`RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean`), meaning only that single chosen credential drives code numbering and subsequent processing. The diff also introduces `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential` which can start writing recovery codes into user storage via `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` without removing any pre-existing local DB recovery-codes credential, making a mixed state (both federated and local credentials present) plausible. In that mixed state, valid codes from the non-selected credential would be ignored/rejected, matching the finding’s described failure mode.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows an unchecked `Optional.get()` in `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean`: it now does `Optional<CredentialModel> credentialModelOpt = RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user);` followed by `credentialModelOpt.get()` with no presence check. Since `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` can return `Optional.empty()` when neither federated nor local recovery-codes credentials exist, this is a concrete, diff-grounded risk of `NoSuchElementException`. However, the claim that this failure is newly exposed by the refactor/flow changes ("old code could not hit") is not verifiable from the diff alone, because the previous code also used `.findFirst().get()` and would similarly throw when no stored credential existed.

adjudication.rationale: In `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage#getCredentials`, the new recovery-codes branch catches `IOException` from `JsonSerialization.readValue(...)`, logs `log.error("Could not deserialize  credential of type: recovery-codes")`, and then simply omits the recovery-codes credential from the returned `Stream` (i.e., returns other credentials only). adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The userStorage fallback writes the raw generated codes as a plain JSON list into the credential's data, but every consumer of the federated credential (RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean, RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator, account REST) parses that data with RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel, which expects the model's own schema (hashed codes, remaining count, next-code numbering) — the two paths disagree on the wire format of the same credential type. adjudication.rationale: The diff does show that `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` passes a JSON array of raw codes via `UserCredentialModel(..., recoveryCodesJson)` when updating user storage. However, the diff also adds `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials(...)`, which *does not* expose that raw JSON-array `CredentialModel` to consumers: it deserializes the stored JSON list and wraps it into a `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` via `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)` before returning it. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The userStorage validation path never consumes or invalidates a used recovery code — isValid() checks the entered code against the full stored list and no code in this diff marks a code as used on the federated path, while the local-storage path decrements remaining codes through RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider. A recovery code captured by an attacker (or shoulder-surfed) grants unlimited logins for a userStorage-backed user, because the same code matches forever; the one-time-use invariant that the local credential model enforces is unrepresentable in the shape CredentialHelper.writeCredential chose (a flat list with no used/remaining state).

adjudication.rationale: In the federated/userStorage path added here, recovery codes are stored as a JSON-serialized flat `List` (CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(): `writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)` and `updateCredential(...)`), and the user-storage validator in `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid(...)` for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE` only checks `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))` without removing/marking the matched code as used or updating stored state. No code in this diff performs any post-success update to consume a used recovery code for the federated credential, so a captured code would continue to validate indefinitely for a userStorage-backed user.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Recovery codes are stored hashed (in the model's secretData) when they land in local storage but as a plaintext JSON list in the userStorage path, so the same logical credential has two divergent representations depending on where it lands. Any userStorage provider adopting this contract inherits a plaintext-copy-of-all-recovery-codes obligation, and code that later migrates, rotates, or audits credentials must handle two formats for one type; the provider author writing updateCredential has no typed contract telling them which shape Keycloak will send.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows two distinct representations being used for the same credential type depending on storage path. In `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)`, the user-storage path serializes `generatedCodes` to a JSON string (`JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)`) and passes it as the `UserCredentialModel` “challengeResponse” (`new UserCredentialModel("", credentialModel.getType(), recoveryCodesJson)`), which user storage providers will receive via `updateCredential`. The finding’s broader concern (user-storage contract ambiguity and divergence) is grounded; however, the claim that local storage is definitively hashed in `secretData` is not shown in this diff, so it can’t be fully verified here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCredential() silently prefers a federated credential over a local one with no detection of, or handling for, both existing, and callers like RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean still call Optional.get() on its result. If a user ever has recovery codes in both stores (e.g. set locally before being linked to userStorage, or a provider that half-handles updateCredential returns false on a later rotation), the stale local copy is silently ignored, and if neither store has the credential the Optional machinery gained in this refactor still ends in an unconditional .get() that throws NoSuchElementException — the Optional adds no safety over the code it replaced.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] updateCredential() is a generic 'update any credential' SPI method being used as a 'create recovery codes' probe — its boolean return means 'the provider handled this credential input', and any userStorage provider that accepts the type but fails internally still returns true, so the local-storage fallback is skipped with no error surfaced. A provider that accepts the recovery-codes type but stores nothing (a stub or partial implementation) causes the required action to report success while the user has no usable credential anywhere — the user is locked out at next login with no error at creation time; there is no verification that what the provider stored is retrievable.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` which first calls `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(recoveryCodesCredential)` and treats the returned boolean as “credential created in user storage”; if `true`, it skips the local-storage creation (`recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(...)`) and does no follow-up verification that a retrievable recovery-codes credential actually exists. However, from the diff alone we can’t verify any concrete provider that would return `true` while persisting nothing (that would be a provider bug/contract violation), so the locked-out scenario is a robustness/architecture concern rather than a demonstrable defect introduced here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential silently discards the hashed RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel when the user storage accepts the credential, persisting the raw generated codes as plaintext JSON instead. For users in a user storage that accepts updateCredential, recovery codes are stored in cleartext (the credentialData field of the UserCredentialModel carries JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)) rather than the hashed representation the required action previously produced, while local-storage users still get hashed credentials — the recovery-codes hashing guarantee established by the existing intent is dropped for the federated path without any explicit acceptance of that downgrade; anyone with read access to the federated store reads usable recovery codes directly.

adjudication.rationale: In CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential, when the federated/user-storage path succeeds (user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...) returns true), it constructs a UserCredentialModel whose “credentialData” is JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes) (i.e., the raw recovery codes in plaintext JSON) and never uses the provided RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel (which would carry the hashed/encoded representation used by the local provider path). The test user-storage implementation also persists input.getChallengeResponse() directly into credentialData, confirming plaintext storage for that path. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The branch for user-storage users writes raw JSON via a bare UserCredentialModel while the fallback branch writes the full hashed credentialModel, producing two incompatible credential shapes for the same credential type with no migration or documented acceptance of the divergence. RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator's getCredential → RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel path now receives, for federated users, a CredentialModel whose credentialData is a raw list of codes rather than the hashed model structure (hashedCodes, remainingCodes, etc.), so the form authenticator's parsing/consumption logic built for the hashed shape operates on a payload it was never designed for — the single-credential-type contract that all consumers assumed is silently forked by this diff.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces two creation paths for the same credential type with different persisted representations. In `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)`, the user-storage path serializes `generatedCodes` to JSON and wraps it in a bare `UserCredentialModel` (`new UserCredentialModel("", credentialModel.getType(), recoveryCodesJson)`) and calls `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`, while the fallback path calls `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel)` using the full `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel`. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The required action's one-time-use semantics for recovery codes are silently dropped for user-storage users: processAction now delegates to createRecoveryCodesCredential, which on the federated path stores the raw code list and never applies the used-code consumption tracking that the local CredentialProvider path applies. adjudication.rationale: The new `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` stores `generatedCodes` as a JSON array string into a `UserCredentialModel` and, if `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` succeeds (federated/user-storage path), it never invokes the local `CredentialProvider#createCredential(...)` with `credentialModel` (which is the only place in this diff where any richer model/semantics could be applied). adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] This diff repurposes BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage — whose documented intent (class javadoc, unchanged in this diff) is to be an unmodified Keycloak-4.8.3-era provider verifying old providers keep working — into an actively extended provider with new recovery-codes support. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] isValid() for recovery codes performs a plain equality match against the stored list but never removes or marks the consumed code as used, making recovery codes infinitely replayable in the federated path. In the local-storage path, Keycloak's RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider invalidates a used code (the credential model's remaining-codes list is decremented on successful auth). The user-storage path added by this diff has no equivalent: the test demonstrates that a federated user can submit the same recovery code on every subsequent login forever, defeating the single-use guarantee that recovery codes exist to provide — an attacker who observes one code (e.g. shoulder-surf or a leaked page) gets permanent second-factor access. The product-side helper (CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential) provides no consumed-code update mechanism for user storage, so this gap is structural, not test-only.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, the newly added federated/user-storage validation path for recovery codes in `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid()` deserializes the stored JSON list and returns `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))` without removing/marking the matched code as consumed or persisting an updated credential (no call to `updateCredential`, no mutation of `myUser.recoveryCodes`, no decrement of remaining codes). That makes a recovery code replayable indefinitely for this user-storage implementation, unlike the intended single-use semantics implied elsewhere (and contrasted by the finding). This behavior is directly verifiable from the added code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The recovery-code comparison generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())) uses a non-constant-time String.equals, and the federated-codes contract it demonstrates exposes raw codes to the provider at all. Whoever copies this pattern as a reference implementation for custom user-storage recovery-code validation inherits both a timing side-channel and plaintext handling of the secret; since Keycloak's local provider compares hashed values with constant-time MessageDigest.isEqual, the federated example silently downgrades the security posture for implementers who mirror it.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce the exact pattern called out: in `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid(...)` the recovery-code check is `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`, which is a normal `String.equals` (not constant-time). The same testsuite provider also stores raw recovery codes as JSON (`recoveryCodesModel.setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse())` and later `JsonSerialization.readValue(..., List.class)`), demonstrating plaintext handling. However, this is in the testsuite/backwards-compatibility user-storage provider (not production code), so it’s not a verifiable product security defect from this diff, but it is a concrete, diff-grounded concern about example/contract patterns for implementers.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin exercises only the happy path of the new federated recovery-code flow and never asserts single-use/invalidation semantics or rejection of a wrong code, so the new isValid/never-consumes behavior in BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java:326-345) is verified only for the success branch. The BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid implementation compares the submitted code against the raw stored list with anyMatch and never removes the used code, while the local-storage provider (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider) invalidates each used code; the test logs in with code index 0 exactly once and asserts only appPage.assertCurrent(), so a regression where federated recovery codes are reusable indefinitely (or where a wrong code is accepted) passes this suite — users of user-storage providers get recovery codes that never burn, an attacker-class weakness in the credential this test claims to certify.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds federated recovery-codes support in the BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage test provider, and its new validation path in `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid(...)` simply deserializes the stored JSON list and returns `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(...)` without removing/invalidating the matched code or updating stored credential state. Nothing else in the shown diff consumes a used recovery code for federated storage. The new test `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` indeed only performs a single successful login using code index 0 and asserts only success, so it would not catch reuse or wrong-code acceptance. Given recovery codes are intended to be single-use, the provider behavior introduced here is a concrete, diff-grounded defect (codes remain reusable indefinitely in this provider).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new fallback branch in CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential (server-spi-private/.../CredentialHelper.java:112-130, the `userStorageCreated == false` path calling recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential) has no test in this diff. Checked BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.java (the only test file changed): all added assertions target a user whose updateCredential returns true, so assertUserDontHaveDBCredentials always runs against the userStorage path; if the fallback-to-local-DB branch regresses (e.g., wrong provider id or dropped credentialModel), the diff's test still passes and a user whose storage declines the credential silently gets no recovery codes at all.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new non-trivial branching logic in `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)`: it first calls `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(recoveryCodesCredential)` and only if that returns `false` it falls back to `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel)`. The only added/modified test (`BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin`) uses `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage`, which was changed to support `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE` and whose `updateCredential(...)` explicitly returns `true` for that type. The test also asserts the user has no DB credentials and that the storage factory has recovery codes, which exercises only the `userStorageCreated == true` path. There is no test in this diff for the fallback-to-local-DB branch (e.g., a user storage that does not support/declines the update), so regressions in the provider-id lookup or fallback call would not be caught by the added coverage.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The IOException catch in BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials swallows the error and silently returns a stream omitting the recovery credential, and no test in the diff triggers a malformed credentialData to verify downstream behavior. If the stored JSON is ever corrupt (e.g., a version skew or the empty-id UserCredentialModel path in CredentialHelper.writeValueAsString changing shape), getCredential in RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils returns Optional.empty and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean throws NoSuchElementException at credentialModelOpt.get() (RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean.java:22) — a 500 on the login page; the swallowing log-only branch means this failure mode is invisible to the diff's green test.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce a silent failure path in the test user-storage provider: `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials(...)` catches `IOException`, logs, and then returns a stream that simply omits the recovery-codes credential (new code in `getCredentials`, `catch (IOException e) { log.error(...); }`). Separately, `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` now calls `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)` and still does `credentialModelOpt.get()` without checking presence, so an omitted/missing credential would throw `NoSuchElementException`. However, the corrupt-JSON scenario is hypothetical and not directly demonstrated by the diff; the finding is primarily about robustness/testing gaps around malformed credential data rather than a clearly reproducible defect introduced here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential passes the plaintext JSON list of raw codes to user storage via UserCredentialModel.getChallengeResponse(), while the local-DB path persists the hashed RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel — the same credential type carries two incompatible payloads depending on which storage handled the write. Any user storage that generically persists the challengeResponse (the documented contract for updateCredential inputs) stores un-hashed codes, and consumers reading via getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream/createFromCredentialModel on such a stored model fail to parse hashed-format credentialData — recovery code validation and display break for those users with no migration path to repair the mixed representations already written.

adjudication.rationale: In `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential`, the user-storage path serializes `generatedCodes` directly (`JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)`) and passes it as a `UserCredentialModel` challengeResponse (`new UserCredentialModel("", credentialModel.getType(), recoveryCodesJson)`), then calls `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)`. The diff shows a user-storage implementation (`BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential`) persisting `input.getChallengeResponse()` into `CredentialModel.credentialData` for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE`, and validating by direct equality against the raw input code. This demonstrates that, at least for such user storages, the new logic stores recovery codes in plaintext JSON rather than the `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` representation used in the local-DB path (`recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel)`). That creates an inconsistency and a security/correctness risk (payload depends on where it’s stored).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The credential is written to exactly one side: when the user storage accepts updateCredential, no local-DB copy of the hashed credential is created, so there is no dual-write during the cutover to federated recovery codes. An operator who later un-links or removes the user storage provider (a standard migration) silently loses every federated user's recovery codes — users fall back to no second factor with no error, a data-loss-on-migration scenario the diff neither backs up nor detects.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly implements a single-write policy in `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)`: it calls `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(recoveryCodesCredential)` and, if that returns true, it *does not* also persist the credential to local DB; only if it returns false does it call `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel)`. That means recovery codes may exist only in federated/user-storage for some users. The finding’s broader “operator later un-links storage and users silently fall back to no second factor” outcome is not directly verifiable from this diff (it depends on migration procedures and flow behavior), but the underlying migration/backup concern (no dual-write / no local copy when federated accepts the update) is real and diff-grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean calls credentialModelOpt.get() on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential, which is empty when a user has no recovery-codes credential in either federated or local storage. A user whose required recovery-codes flow reaches this bean without a credential (e.g., the credential was deleted between the required action and the login, or a storage returns an empty getCredentials stream) gets an unhandled NoSuchElementException and a 500 login page instead of a fallback to another authenticator in the alternative subflow.

adjudication.rationale: In `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` the constructor now does `Optional<CredentialModel> credentialModelOpt = RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user);` and then immediately calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` to build the `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel`. From the diff, `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)` can legitimately return `Optional.empty()` when neither `getFederatedCredentialsStream()` nor `getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...)` contains a recovery-codes credential. In that case, `get()` will throw `NoSuchElementException` and there is no handling in this bean, so the failure would be an unhandled runtime exception rather than a controlled/authenticator-level fallback.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] isValid for the recovery-codes type compares the entered code against the stored plain list and never consumes or updates the stored credential, so recovery codes validated through the user storage remain valid forever. The test asserts the happy-path login works, but the single-use semantics that the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider enforces (used-code counters in the credential data) are silently lost for federated users — anyone replaying a captured recovery code on the federated path is accepted, and tests built on this provider will pass while production semantics diverge.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds recovery-codes support to the federated test provider `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage`. In `isValid(...)`, the new `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE` branch deserializes the stored JSON list and returns `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`, but it never updates the stored credential to mark a code as used or remove it. Given the intended recovery-code behavior implied elsewhere in the diff (e.g., `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.getNextRecoveryAuthnCode()` usage in `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean`), this means a recovery code validated via this user-storage path can be replayed indefinitely, diverging from typical single-use semantics and potentially masking issues in tests using this provider.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] createRecoveryCodesCredential wraps the IOException from JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString in a bare RuntimeException, aborting the required-action with an unhandled 500 after the user has already been shown the one-time recovery codes. If JSON serialization of the generated codes list fails, the user's browser shows the recovery codes page, clicks save, and gets a raw 500 (no INVALID_CREDENTIALS/controlled challenge, no error page per the required-action contract); the codes were displayed but never persisted, and the required action is silently left pending, so the user is stuck in a loop of generating codes that are never stored.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` serializes `generatedCodes` via `JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)` and on `IOException` throws `new RuntimeException(e)` (server-spi-private/.../CredentialHelper.java). This method is invoked from the required action `RecoveryAuthnCodesAction.processAction(...)` without any handling (services/.../RecoveryAuthnCodesAction.java), so an `IOException` would propagate as an unhandled server error rather than a controlled required-action challenge/response. That would abort persistence after the user already obtained/displayed codes, leaving the required action pending.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] When the user storage accepts the credential (userStorageCreated == true), the hashed RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel is discarded and the plaintext generated codes are delivered via challengeResponse, so any user storage implementing updateCredential persists the raw codes with no hashed form anywhere. For user-storage users, the only persisted copy of recovery codes is the plaintext JSON in challengeResponse. When the credential is later consumed (a code used at login), Keycloak's consumption path updates via a RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel whose serialized credentialData is the hashed format, and the storage's later getCredentials/isValid deserializes it as List.class — readValue(List.class) on the hashed JSON object structure fails (IOException path) or the codes never match, so single-use consumption silently breaks for federated users after the first code use.

adjudication.rationale: In `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)`, when `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(recoveryCodesCredential)` returns true, the code never persists the provided `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel credentialModel` (presumably the canonical/hashed representation) and instead sends `recoveryCodesJson = JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)` as the `challengeResponse` in a `UserCredentialModel`. The diff also updates the federated test storage (`BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential`) to persist `input.getChallengeResponse()` directly into `CredentialModel.credentialData`, i.e., storing the raw JSON list of codes. This makes the only stored copy for federated users plaintext (and different from the credential-model-based representation), which is a concrete, diff-verifiable correctness/security issue. The later-consumption mismatch described is plausible but not fully verifiable from this diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCredential prefers the federated credential unconditionally and only falls back to local storage when no federated credential exists, so a user with both a stale local recovery-codes credential and a fresh federated one authenticates against whichever the federated lookup returns first with no staleness check. Operators migrating a user from user storage to local storage (or vice versa) end up with two live recovery-code sets; the hidden one remains valid for the form authenticator's updateCredential-driven consumption path and for account-REST delete operations targeting the local credential, leaving an orphaned still-usable credential that no one can enumerate.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(UserModel)` which explicitly returns the first *federated* recovery-codes credential if any exists, and only then falls back to `getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...)` (local DB) (see `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils#getCredential`). In parallel, the new `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential(...)` may create/update a federated credential via `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` but does not remove any existing local recovery-codes credential when that succeeds, meaning both can coexist. This can lead to a “hidden” second credential set depending on which storage you query first. However, the finding’s stronger claims about “no one can enumerate” the other credential and about account-REST delete/consumption semantics are not verifiable from this diff alone (those code paths are not shown), so it’s best treated as an architectural/edge-case concern rather than a proven defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The rewritten constructor still calls credentialModelOpt.get() on an Optional that getCredential can return empty, throwing NoSuchElementException instead of a controlled failure. A user whose recovery-codes credential is deleted (or whose user storage returns it via a path that isConfiguredFor accepts but getCredential filters out, e.g. a type-mismatched federated record) reaches the login form renderer and gets a raw 500 from template rendering rather than the configured invalid-credentials challenge.

adjudication.rationale: In `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean` the constructor now does `Optional<CredentialModel> credentialModelOpt = RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user);` and immediately calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` with no presence check. `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` can return `Optional.empty()` if neither a federated nor stored recovery-codes credential exists, which would throw `NoSuchElementException` during page/model rendering (uncaught in this code path).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCredentials silently drops the recovery-codes credential on deserialization failure, logging a message without the exception or username and still returning the OTP-only stream. If myUser.recoveryCodes.getCredentialData() is corrupt (e.g. after a consumption update stores the hashed JSON format that readValue(List.class) cannot parse), the user appears to have no recovery codes at all: isConfiguredFor still returns true (it checks the raw field) but the credential stream is empty, so getCredential() returns empty and the login bean throws NoSuchElementException — a silent partial-success state that the error log alone makes undiagnosable.

adjudication.rationale: In BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage#getCredentials, recovery codes are deserialized via JsonSerialization.readValue(..., List.class) inside a try/catch; on IOException it only logs `log.error("Could not deserialize  credential of type: recovery-codes")` and does not add the credential to the returned stream, while still returning OTP credentials if present. Meanwhile isConfiguredFor checks only `myUser.recoveryCodes != null` and can return true even when getCredentials omits the recovery-codes credential. This inconsistency can propagate to RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils#getCredential(user) (which depends on credential streams) returning empty, and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean then calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` without presence checks, leading to NoSuchElementException. The log also omits the exception and username, making the failure hard to diagnose.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] isValid for recovery codes matches the submitted code against the full stored list without ever removing or marking the used code, so recovery codes are infinitely reusable. Any generated code authenticates the federated user an unlimited number of times, defeating the single-use guarantee the recovery-codes feature promises; the new test logs in once and never asserts a second use of the same code fails, so this regression is invisible to the suite.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added test user-storage implementation, `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid(...)` for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE` deserializes the stored JSON list and returns `anyMatch` against `input.getChallengeResponse()` without updating/removing the used code (no mutation is shown in this diff). Also, the new test `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` performs only a single successful login using one recovery code and never attempts to reuse the same code to assert it is rejected, so it wouldn’t catch a single-use regression in the federated-storage path. However, the diff does not show whether core recovery-code logic consumes codes via a subsequent `updateCredential(...)` call, so the claim of “infinitely reusable” cannot be verified solely from this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] hasRecoveryCodes looks up userPasswords.get(username) directly, bypassing the translateUserName normalization every other access path in the storage applies. If the user is created or stored under a differently-cased name than the assertion helper passes, the factory returns false for a user who does have recovery codes, making assertUserHasRecoveryKeysCredentialInUserStorage fail (or pass vacuously) with no signal that the lookup itself was wrong.

adjudication.rationale: In BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage, accesses to the internal users map go through translateUserName(user.getUsername()) (e.g., updateCredential() and getMyUser()), implying usernames may be normalized for storage. The newly added BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageFactory.hasRecoveryCodes(String username) does a direct userPasswords.get(username) lookup without any normalization, mirroring hasUserOTP. This can make the test assertion helper return false for a user that exists if the caller uses a differently-cased username, potentially leading to misleading test outcomes rather than a production defect.
